This review is from the rather casual perspective of a guy who finished every level once with a group of friends and has zero desire to replay and master it for hundreds of hours, so keep that in mind.

That being said - yeah, it’s really fun when it’s just being Left 4 Dead but Warhammer 40K. Slicing through giant, juicy waves of cannon fodder while being thrown into frantic panic situations by minibosses is highly entertaining and enjoyable. Also, the godlike soundtrack by my boi Jesper Kyd cements that sense of drive with a bow on top. A+ stuff.

It’s what sets it apart from Left 4 Dead that I have a problem with.

First of all, the levels are just way too dаmn long. I really don’t know what stopped them from just putting checkpoint saferooms-style in elevators that already split the level into several smaller areas. Without them, the game just kinda forces us to sleepwalk through like 25 minutes of been-there-done-that filler to get to the actually challenging bits on replays.

Second, the amount of upgradeables in this game is absurdly comical. You can upgrade every little thing in like five different ways in five different parts of the hub, and it absolutely becomes cumbersome after a while. I don’t see a valid reason not to have one «upgrade guy» and one «buy-or-upgrade gun» page right in the main menu and leave it at that. All it did for me as it stands now is discourage me from ever changing my gun at the thought of having to run around through all this nonsense again.

The game has a lot of throwing things at a wall and seeing what sticks in general. I don’t know whose bright idea it was to put optional pace-braking puzzles in this fast-paced shooter, but here they are. At least they are optional, and you can eventually persuade your party to stop wasting your time on them.

Last but certainly not least - this game’s dialogue system is downright hostile to groups that play the whole game with the same set of characters. It works fine with randos, but in the same party, the same long-аss dialogues start repeating so gratingly often that third-party please-shut-up-already mods are kind of a must. This problem sounds petty, but it really is not. It is so dаmn annoying.

It is still a fine enough game overall, and I might return to it if they release some new maps.

The art style and gameplay is unbeatable but this game has its flaws people need to be aware of. A lot of people report that the game runs terribly on even the beefiest machines and I can assure you it 100% has that issue. I don't have the issue as bad as some report but after about 6-7 hours straight your frames will start to drop, telling you that its time to restart the game and let memory reset or something. My PC is not that powerful and I run this game on the highest quality just fine. The other issue with this game is that the player base can just be really terrible some times. The game is very active and its not hard to find good friends to play this with, BUT I have been on teams that would want to make you suck on a 12 gauge. At time allies won't do the only objective or pay attention, and I or some other player with at least some common sense has to come and save the day. This game is a lot like destiny's raid system. You and a fireteam take on a variety of enemies and move about a linear level while completing brain dead easy objectives. The difficulty is the in the swarms of enemies sort of like Left4Dead. You will be placed into matches of people that have put dozen of hours in and leveled characters, only to see them all stand there, not dodge, barely put up a fight, and now everyone is down but you. In this game it is possible to take on a majority of the enemies yourself but its definitely not made to be played that way, and a lot of the time it doesn't work out. Either way this game is really incredible and it deserves players that want to get in, commit, and have an awesome experience. The game is not hard whatsoever and if you want character builds YouTube is your best friend. My only advice is this is a team based game, be a productive part of your team. The Good:
The actual core combat loop in Warhammer 40,000: Darktide is phenomenal. Fatshark’s hybrid ranged-and-melee gunplay feels incredibly visceral, the 40K atmosphere is top-notch, and slicing through hordes of Nurgle cultists with a chainsword is addicting when it actually runs smoothly.

The Bad:
The technical implementation on PC—especially for AMD users—is an absolute disaster.

Engine Bottlenecks & Threading Chaos: The game runs on Fatshark’s abandoned Autodesk Stingray engine, and it struggles with thread management. On an 8-core CPU (like the 7800X3D), you literally have to go into the launcher options and manually tweak worker threads just to stop the game from micro-stuttering every time a horde spawns.

Ray Tracing is Broken on AMD: Even on current-gen hardware built to handle RT, turning on Ray Tracing (RTGI / Reflections) completely kills your framerate. The game lacks proper BVH traversal optimizations for AMD architecture, forcing high-end cards to tank a ~40% performance hit while overloading the CPU during wave spawns.

Severe Performance Scaling Issues: Instead of scaling smoothly, dense particle effects, volumetric fog, and ragdoll physics cause violent frametime spikes. You are forced to disable key graphical features and rely heavily on upscalers like FSR just to get a stable frame rate.

Verdict:
Darktide is a fantastic co-op shooter buried under terrible engine architecture. If you run AMD hardware and expect to turn on Ray Tracing or get seamless out-of-the-box performance without digging into launcher settings and disabling half the graphical features, skip this one.

The best thing to know about this game going in is it's about mastery. There are other modes, but by far the focus is on its main mode: playing missions on higher and higher difficulties, getting good enough to handle whatever is thrown at you, and chasing the incredible high of clutching at the peak of chaos.

STORY

You start (assuming you don't take one of the DLC classes first) as a reject, a prisoner stuck in a cell near a captured rebel captain Wolfer from the Moebian 6th, an infantry unit turned traitor after one hellish assignment too many. Their alignment to Nurgle leads to Wolfer getting broken out, and your cell being collateral. An operative for the inquisition, Explicator Zola, sees you're out and, needing help dealing with the traitors in the prison area, recruits you to help get out of there. From there, you'll go through a basic tutorial and find yourself on the Mourningstar, a ship held by rogue trader Mistress Brahm, with a portion of it unhappily lent to the Inquisition to quell a rapidly growing turn to Nurgle across Atoma Prime's main hive city, Tertium. You're not trusted, but Zola's been recruiting prisoners lately as expendable operatives. Welcome aboard. You're not important, but you might be of use.

If that story element grabs you, great! Just be sure to pay tons of attention, as the story's given in a Souls-like manner: through snippets of dialogue before, during and after missions that you need to piece together to get a clearer picture. It's an excellent look at the Imperium of Mankind through the lens of competing administrative branches, disagreeing about the best way to handle a problem and struggling to work together, with you in the middle.

GAMEPLAY

At its peak, Darktide absolutely surrounds you with enemies of all types, and organising the chaos is your test. Dodging disables, ranged enemies that can wipe you out in a moment's notice, and enemies filling the floor with fire or toxic gas limiting your options. There'll always be a way out of it, but figuring out how in the mania is the challenge, and managing it feels electric. At its worst, you'll feel like you had no chance as you're grabbed, slammed into fire, and thrown into an enemy that explodes, putting you down in a couple of seconds, while enemies with chain axes quickly wipe away the short time you have to be put back on your feet by allies. There was always a way around it, but it can be hard to rationalise that when the game throws everything at you.

The game doesn't do a great job of preparing you for the near infinite skill ceiling you face: early difficulties can feel hard if you're not familiar with the horde shooter genre, and the game's melee focus may challenge players even then. Teamplay is incredibly important as you progress, and getting your character to level 30 is fun, but it's only the start - and that's a great thing, as there's a deep well of decisions to work from once you hit it. Just be aware you can get away with parting from your team and taking fights in open areas in lower difficulties. You'll be sorely punished for it later on. Avoiding learning bad habits from your first few dozen hours can help make the learning curve feel less rough. In almost every mission, situations that feel impossible can be overcome with the right approach.

SYSTEMS 

You've got a lot of choice in the way of customisation and fine tuning. Classes play notably both between each other and between differing builds. The weapons and blessing you pick make a world of difference, and striving to find the best way to make a weapon you like work well is deeply satisfying once it all clicks. Each class has three diverging talent paths you can generally pick and choose from to rework your build, with a ton of weapon choices. Each weapon has 20 levels of mastery earned from using them in missions, the levelling of which allows you to unlock various blessings to amend your weapon's traits, unlock different versions of the base weapon, and improve its power. 

One problem with the game is its communication to the player of its systems. There's a ton to the game, but relatively little of it is explained outright, much like its story. A great example is the weapon upgrade system, which is somewhat confusing at first. As you level up your mastery, you put points into unlocking and upgrading blessings you can then add to a weapon, which you can raise from a basic grey profane level with no additional improvements to a transcendent weapon with two blessings and two refinements. The blessings you can choose are purely what you've put your points into from levelling up the weapon. No weapon can be perfect; each weapon's stats can go up to 80/80, with one stat out of those reaching only 60/80, or having that 20 point deficit spread across multiple stats. 

Players typically identify what stat they want to "dump", then buy the weapon with the in game currency until one with the right maximum stats appear, to upgrade it to the maximum strength and apply the blessings they want. Weekly contracts assigning given tasks (collect a resource, complete 8 missions, kill 1000 of a group of enemy) help provide a currency that allow you to quickly pick up a good weapon to work with, either to try out, level up with or to use as best fit - minor stat distribution differences won't matter much until the hardest difficulties the game has to throw at you in Havoc mode. Great players will insist you can win anything but the hardest difficulties with anything, but until you're that good, you'll feel when a weapon does a great job against the current balancing, or when it falls short.

Besides that, you can unlock cosmetic elements by completing "penances", an in-game achievement system that tracks your feats across each class the game has to offer, and in each mission and game type. The rewards are mostly for the four base classes of psyker, ogryn, veteran or zealot, but titles, trinkets to put on your weapon and skins for some weapons are shareable across applicable DLC classes. 

DLC

The DLC for this game gives you more ways to play via its additional classes. The Adeptus Arbites make for tanky, staggering front liners, performing a similar role to the ogryn, with a cyber-mastiff to assist you in most of its potential build. 

The Hive Scum are hyper mobile glass cannons in theory, though their slipperiness can make them extremely survivable, where the potential for maximising damage is enormous. They allow for a focus either on direct damage via critical hits or a team-buffing focus on stimms and damage over time. Their speed allow you to play the game at the pace of your reactions, rather than any limits from your character.

The Skitarii are highly adaptable tech-infused warriors, focused around electrocuting or burning your enemies, with a servo-skull to assist in helping allies, solving tech issues and shooting down opponents quickly.

MODS

Another major boon is the developer's positivity towards mods. Don't like an element of the UI? Look up mods, there'll be a way to change it. Where the devs can be slow to add QoL, the modders have you covered. Most things that you might find frustrating can be amended. Navigate to particular menus instantly instead of running around the Mourningstar. See mission details as you drop in to know what you're getting into from quickly. Clearer details in your talent trees and on your weapons. AoEs highlighted, enemy details - whatever you want, it's available.

It's an absolute blast of a game, and a joy to feel yourself improving at. Give it a try, know the difficulty you start with is nothing like what you're going to face eventually, and you'll fall in love in no time.

Hot take: For every £10 a game costs, it should offer roughly 100 hours of fresh content.

Darktide has about 60 hours of genuine content before you start "eating the sawdust in the cereal" so to speak. That 60 hours covers mastering the one class and loadout you actually enjoy, unlocking the cosmetics you like, and clearing all the interesting/challenging missions on the highest difficulties. 

After that, you’re mostly repeating the same mission tiles, fishing for penances, or forcing yourself to level weapons and classes you don’t care about.

Yes, you can replay every mission again, try every weapon/class, or grind every penance. If that’s your idea of fun, go for it. But that isn’t fresh content — it’s the same content on loop. Once you’ve experienced the peak, the remaining checklist starts to feel like filler.

I got it for £7 on sale and I’m happy with the time I spent. 

At full RRP, I wouldn’t recommend it unless you’re the type who enjoys endless repetition of the same missions. The core combat is excellent, especially if you find a playstyle that clicks the way the combat blade did for me, but the overall package runs out of new things to do surprisingly fast if you’re even slightly above average at these kinds of games.

I have been playing on and off since release. Of course, at release everyone knows it was a bit rough, but the bones were solid, the game was fun, and the world was beautiful.

But 3 years later and it's definitely been a recurrent time sink with friends and family. Fatshark consistently provides content updates, improvements and polish passes, while only ever asking money through optional character DLC that are worthwhile all on their own.

As a returning or new player, the game does not confuse you with thousands of pop ups and options, it throws you directly into the gameplay loop and never loses focus on what you're there to do in the first place. Group up with friends, shoot some xeno heretical scum and get some loot and skill tree upgrades.

Sure there's other modes, challenge modifiers and specific achievements to go for, but it never feels overwhelming, or like what you're specifically doing is sub-optimal to have an enjoyable or complete experience. It's just a very well rounded, paced, organized and focused game.

[b] The one con [/b]

I will concede that Fatshark has in fact made the game run better, smoother, more consistent and generally with much higher fps and lower requirements overall. But as someone with a pretty strong pc, i find it a little annoying that the ray tracing implementation is rather underwhelming, and causes heavy performance drawbacks. Remember that this is a game that already can dip in relatively low fps during intense hordes (which is reasonable), so having a *fancy* feature that doesnt really add much (i suppose this is partially a compliment to the original art and visual design made by the talented artists at the studio) which also tanks the fps that drastically, forcing you to use Frame-Gen to have acceptable FPS at the cost of yet again a flaring drawback; input latency, is kind of dissapointing.

I suppose you can view this positively as a testament to the original art direction being so strong and well conceived that Ray tracing provides little advantages, and therefore feels like an unworthy tradeoff for the performance cost.

Forget being a Space Marine. Give me a knife, a gun, and a terrible attitude — I'm going in.

Warhammer 40,000: Darktide is one of those games that just feels incredible to play.

You're thrown into the filthy, oppressive depths of a hive city and told to go deal with whatever nightmare the Imperium has decided is your problem today. You're not some legendary hero. You're a reject, a scumbag, a nobody — and somehow that makes tearing through hordes of heretics even more satisfying.

I've been playing as a Hive Scum, and I absolutely love the feel and gameplay of the class. There's something incredibly satisfying about carving your way through a horde with a melee weapon one second and then unloading a gun into something horrible the next. The movement, weapon animations, impacts and sound design all come together to make every hit feel weighty and vicious.

And then the game throws fifty enemies at you.

That's where Darktide really comes alive.

You can be calmly moving through the hive one moment and, seconds later, you're surrounded by screaming cultists, mutants, specialists and armoured monstrosities while you and your team are desperately trying to keep each other alive.

The combat has this fantastic rhythm of shoot, dodge, block, shove, slice, reposition, and repeat. You're constantly making split-second decisions about whether to push forward, fall back, reload, revive a teammate or just start swinging and hope for the best.

And playing it with friends?

That's where the magic happens.

Darktide is at its best when four friends are screaming over voice chat while everything has gone completely to hell. Someone gets grabbed. Someone else is down. The horde is coming. You're almost out of ammunition. Then someone pulls off a clutch revive and suddenly you're all fighting your way through together.

Those moments are so much fun.

The game also nails the Warhammer 40,000 atmosphere. The gigantic hive city, industrial machinery, religious fanaticism, endless corridors and sheer oppressive scale make you feel like you're actually wandering through the grim darkness of the far future. You're not saving the galaxy because you're special.

You're just trying to survive your shift.

And somehow, that makes every victory feel better.

Darktide is brutal, loud, disgusting, ridiculously satisfying and incredibly fun with friends. The combat feels fantastic, the weapons have real personality, and the sheer chaos of a mission can produce some of the funniest and most memorable moments you'll have in a co-op game.

If you've ever wanted to experience 40K from the perspective of the poor bastard who gets sent into the hive when everyone more important is too busy arguing about what to do...

Welcome to Darktide, reject.

An absolute blast wrapped in a ticking time bomb of broken code.
First off, huge thanks to my brother for gifting me this game—the core cooperative gameplay, combat loop, and atmosphere are genuinely incredible. When you drop into a match, the action is top-tier. My PC completely destroys it at 1080p on extreme settings using frame generation, delivering buttery-smooth performance right out of the gate.
The problem is the unmitigated memory leak cancer plaguing this engine.
No matter how high-end your hardware is or how well you brute-force your settings at the start of a session, the game suffers from a severe cumulative degradation loop. Over the course of a mission, background assets and script data fail to flush out, slowly choking your buffers until the frame pacing collapses right before extraction. You are forced to manually restart the entire application just to clear the pipes, acting as an unpaid QA tester for an optimization issue that has persisted for years.
It drives me insane seeing positive reviews brush this under the rug or act like brute-forcing high frame rates on a powerful GPU means the game is fine. Having expensive hardware doesn't excuse lazy optimization or broken garbage collection. If you love visceral combat, the game is great—just be ready to restart your game constantly because the backend architecture is fundamentally rotting from the inside out.

Easy 7.5/10 at full price and 8/10 on sale. The gameplay is very, very close to Left 4 Dead, just set in the Warhammer universe. If you enjoy that style of game, you’ll probably love cleansing heretics in Darktide.

I do have a few personal complaints. First, the game needs a proper solo mode. A mod already exists that allows solo play and makes the bots genuinely useful, so there is no reason the developers couldn’t add something similar officially.

The game also needs a proper campaign and a clearer story. The missions are connected, but the overall narrative is often difficult to follow. A simple Chapter 1 through 15 structure, with cutscenes tying everything together, would make a huge difference.

They also need to add some mega-bosses. Right now, most of the bosses feel pretty weak, even on the higher difficulties. The characters could also use far more customization.

The rotating shop needs to go because I hate that system sooooo much. Shop currency should also be earnable through gameplay. I understand that Fatshark needs to make extra money, but there should be a reasonable option for the average player. Maybe limit players to earning 250 credits per week. It would still take several weeks to unlock a full cosmetic package, but at least players would have another way to get one.

Lastly, the game needs another full campaign because it simply needs more levels. There are plenty of other minor things I could complain about, but nothing that ruins the experience. Some players constantly rush past everything, which is incredibly annoying, but that isn’t really the game’s fault. If anything, the game strongly encourages teamwork because staying together makes every level much easier.

Overall, it’s a great game, and I enjoy it just as much as Helldivers and Left 4 Dead. I can only imagine how incredible the ultimate horde shooter would be: Darktide’s combat and atmosphere combined with Helldivers’ movement and animations.

Hey kiddo, Handsome Jack here... and I just played Warhammer 40,000: Darktide, and apparently the Imperium has developed a revolutionary new employee management strategy: take four complete lunatics, throw them into a city infested with thousands of diseased cultists, and tell them to keep killing until management is satisfied.

Finally.

A workplace environment I understand.

You start as some nobody prisoner and somehow get recruited into the Imperial war machine. Congratulations! You've been promoted from “criminal” to “expendable asset.”

That's career progression.

Then they hand you a weapon and send you into a hive city where everything is trying to kill you. Cultists, mutants, flamethrower guys, snipers, giant monsters, screaming lunatics...

And approximately seven million enemies per square meter.

You kill one.

Another appears.

You kill ten.

A horde arrives.

You kill the horde.

ANOTHER HORDE.

At some point I'm convinced the Imperium is manufacturing these guys just so I have something to shoot.

The combat is fantastic, though. Guns feel powerful, melee combat feels brutal, and there's something deeply satisfying about taking a giant sword and turning an entire crowd of enemies into a very complicated meat salad.

And the chainsword?

OH, KIDDO.

That thing doesn't kill people.

It files them under “no longer employed.”

Then there's the team.

You've got the Veteran, who shoots everything.

The Zealot, who screams about the Emperor while hitting things with religious enthusiasm.

The Ogryn, who is essentially a giant lovable refrigerator with a grenade launcher.

And the Psyker, who can literally explode someone's head with their mind.

This is a perfectly balanced workplace.

No HR department required.

And the voice lines are fantastic. Everyone sounds miserable. Which makes sense because they're working for the Imperium.

You finish a mission and instead of getting a bonus, you get told:

“Good. Do it again.”

Kiddo.

That's not employment.

That's slavery with extra steps.

The atmosphere is incredible too. The hive city feels gigantic, filthy, oppressive, and completely hopeless. Everything is covered in rust, blood, machinery, and religious propaganda.

It's beautiful.

It's basically a Hyperion facility after the cleaning staff quit.

The game does have its problems. Progression and loot systems can be frustrating, missions can start feeling repetitive, and sometimes you spend more time waiting around than you'd like.

But when the music kicks in, the horde comes charging toward you, your team forms a defensive line, and everyone starts screaming while thousands of enemies crash into you?

That's the good stuff.

9/10, kiddo.

Fantastic combat, incredible atmosphere, ridiculous enemies, and some of the best co-op chaos you'll find.

I'd give it a 10, but apparently the Imperium doesn't offer dental coverage.

And I'm not working for an employer who can't provide basic employee benefits.

Even if the employer is technically an immortal corpse sitting on a golden toilet.

That's just bad management.

I enjoy Darktide's core gameplay, atmosphere, music, and depiction of 40K enormously. Unfortunately, there is one aspect of its character writing that has become increasingly difficult for me to overlook: the game's remarkably conspicuous treatment of sex.

Consider the recurring friendly authority figures:

Inquisitor Grendyl — Unknown
Interrogator Rannick — Male
Interrogator Inigo — Female
Explicator Zola — Female
Sergeant-Major Morrow — Male
Hadron Omega-7-7 — Female
Sefoni — Female
Flight Lieutenant Masozi — Female
Sire Melk — Male
Quartermaster Brunt — Male
Sister Prine — Female
Shipmistress Brahms — Female
Commodore Hallowette — Female
Enginseer Kayex-8 — Male
Commissar Dukane — Female
Mara Vinci — Female

Excluding the deliberately mysterious Grendyl, that is 10 women and 5 men: **two-thirds female**.

I don't object to women holding these positions. This is Warhammer 40,000. Female Inquisitors, commissars, officers, Rogue Traders, soldiers and other figures of authority are perfectly ordinary parts of the setting. Nor do I expect a fictional cast to conform precisely to real-world demographics. A 50/50 cast wouldn't bother me in the slightest.

What bothers me is the aggregate pattern.

The player spends an enormous amount of time being instructed, supervised, evaluated and supplied by a conspicuously female-heavy collection of authority figures, while the human enemies the player spends hundreds of hours shooting, burning, exploding and dismembering appear overwhelmingly male.

Any individual casting decision is perfectly defensible. It is the cumulative effect that becomes difficult not to notice.

If the pattern were reversed—if roughly two-thirds of the friendly authority figures were men while the disposable human enemies being slaughtered by the thousands were overwhelmingly women—I suspect the representational implications would attract considerable criticism. I don't see why the reverse arrangement should be immune from the same scrutiny.

I am not claiming that Fatshark hates men, nor can I know the writers' intentions. Perhaps nobody consciously intended this pattern at all. But authorial intention doesn't change what eventually appears on the screen.

And that is ultimately my problem with it: **I can see the casting decisions behind the characters.**

Good fantasy makes me forget that somebody designed the world. When demographic patterns become sufficiently conspicuous that I start anticipating the sex of the next commander, expert, superior or disposable enemy, my suspension of disbelief has been damaged. Instead of seeing the Imperium of Man, I start seeing a modern writing room deciding who should occupy which narrative roles.

Darktide is otherwise exceptionally good at making its world feel authentic. Its environments are magnificent, its combat is superb, its soundtrack is outstanding, and at its best it captures the grotesque grandeur of 40K better than almost any other game.

That's precisely why this bothers me. I don't want contemporary political fashions to be visible through the fiction. I want Atoma to feel like Atoma—not like the Democratic National Convention wandered into the 41st Millennium.

Keep contemporary partisan politics out of games, unless you want to watch your long-time fans bail while the “modern audience” you're fishing for never materializes.
